name: Arrays & Hashing
analogy: A coat check takes your coat and hands you a ticket. Later you show the ticket and your coat comes back at once, with nobody searching the rack. A hash map is the same trade: spend a little memory and every lookup is instant.
whenToUse: You check the same values again and again
Counts, pairs or duplicates decide the answer
Brute force compares every pair of items

transcript.text: Two Sum asks which two numbers add to 9. Trying every pair means each number meets every other number. That is n² work.
Instead, walk the list once and keep a map of numbers you have seen. Each entry remembers a number and the index where it sits.
For each number, ask the map for its partner. 9 minus 7 is 2, and 2 is already in the map, so the pair is 0 and 1.
One pass, one map lookup each: O(n) time. That is arrays and hashing: memory traded for instant lookups.

name: Two Pointers
idea: Two indices walking toward an answer.

name: Sliding Window
idea: A range that grows and shrinks as it scans.
analogy: Look out of a train window. New scenery slides in on the right, old scenery slides out on the left, and you never re-read the whole view. You only deal with what changed.
whenToUse: The answer is a contiguous run (subarray or substring)
It asks for the longest, shortest or a count
Brute force is two nested loops

transcript.text: Say you need the longest stretch of a string with no repeated letters. The obvious way checks every start and every end. That’s n² work.
Instead, keep a window. Move its right edge one letter at a time and remember what’s inside.
When a letter repeats, slide the left edge forward until the repeat is gone. The window never moves backwards.
Each letter enters once and leaves once. One pass, O(n). That’s the sliding window.

name: Stack
idea: Remember the past, answer on the way back.
analogy: Think of a stack of plates. You only ever touch the top one, and the last plate you put down is the first one you pick up.

name: Binary Search
idea: Halve the search space every step.

name: Linked List
idea: Rewire pointers without losing the chain.

name: Tries
idea: Share prefixes, find words letter by letter.
analogy: Start typing a word and your phone narrows the guesses with every letter. After two letters you are already on the right page for every word that starts that way. A trie stores words the same way, sharing each prefix once so a lookup only walks the letters you type.
whenToUse: The task is prefix search or autocomplete
Many words share the same beginnings
Lookups must cost one step per letter

transcript.text: Searching a word list means checking every word from its first letter. When thousands of words share beginnings, all that repeated reading adds up.
A trie stores each shared beginning once. “apple” and “app” walk the same a-p-p path and branch only where they differ.
Inserting reuses every node already there, then marks where the word ends. Looking up “app” walks the same path letter by letter.
Each operation costs one hop per letter: O(L). That’s the trie.

name: Heaps
analogy: Picture a line of people sorted by height, split into two teams at the middle. The shorter team only watches its tallest member, and the taller team only its shortest. The median is always where the two teams meet, so nobody ever sorts the whole line.
whenToUse: Items arrive one at a time, unsorted
You need the middle, min or max so far
Brute force sorts after every arrival

transcript.text: Numbers arrive one at a time and you must report the median after each. Sorting everything so far each time costs n log n per number.
Instead, split the numbers into a lower half and an upper half. Each half only watches the member closest to the split.
15 arrives and lands in the lower half, then the biggest of that half moves across. Both tops read 5 and 15, so the median is 10.
Each number costs one heap push and pop: O(log n). That’s the two-heap median.

name: Backtracking
analogy: Walk into a maze with a piece of chalk. When you hit a dead end, step back to the last fork and try the next turn, never walking the same dead end twice. Backtracking explores choices the same way, undoing each step so every option gets exactly one visit.
whenToUse: You must list every valid arrangement
Each step tries one of a few options
A wrong turn can be undone cleanly

transcript.text: Which sets of 2, 3, 6 and 7 add to 7? Trying every multiset blindly repeats dead ends, because most sets overshoot or miss.
Try one number at a time and carry what is left. Each choice narrows the question to a smaller target.
2, 2 then 3 reaches exactly 7, so [2, 2, 3] is saved. With only 1 left, 2 is already too big, so that whole branch is cut.
Trying every branch is exponential, but each cut prunes a whole subtree. That’s backtracking.

name: Graphs
idea: Explore neighbours with BFS and DFS.
analogy: Drop ink on any land square you have not coloured yet. It spreads to every square joined to it, but never crosses water. Each drop is one island, and counting the drops counts the islands.
whenToUse: The input is a grid or a network
Answers spread through neighbours
You must count joined-up regions

transcript.text: A grid of land and water hides joined-up islands. Re-exploring from every land cell repeats the same ground over and over.
Scan row by row instead. The first unclaimed land, at row 0, col 0, must be a new island.
A queue floods from it to every joined square, claiming island 1. The scan moves on and finds two more.
Each cell is claimed once: O(m·n). Three drops of ink, three islands. That’s graph search.

name: 1-D DP
analogy: Plan a route of jobs in a notebook, one line per day. Each line holds the best total so far, so tomorrow’s choice only looks at the last two lines. The final line is the answer, built without ever redoing a day.
whenToUse: Today’s answer builds on yesterday’s
Brute force retries the same subproblem
You only need the last few answers

transcript.text: Five houses hold 2, 7, 9, 3 and 1, but neighbours share an alarm. Trying every subset rechecks the same endings again and again.
Write down the best haul for the first house, then the first two. Each answer only needs the two lines above it.
At house 3, skipping keeps 7 but taking adds 9 to 2. Taking wins, so dp[3] is 11.
One pass fills the row: O(n). The last cell reads 12, from houses 1, 3 and 5. That’s 1-D DP.

name: 2-D DP
idea: Fill a table cell by cell.
analogy: Picture a spreadsheet where every formula only points at the cells above and to the left. Fill it from the top-left corner and each cell becomes a small finished answer. The bottom-right cell then holds the whole answer, built without redoing a single cell.
whenToUse: Two strings or grids must be compared
Each answer builds on smaller prefixes
Brute force checks every pair of prefixes

transcript.text: “abcde” and “ace” share letters in order, but which run is longest? Listing every subsequence of each word explodes fast.
Build a table instead. Each cell answers a smaller question: how much do these two prefixes share?
Fill it corner to corner. ‘c’ meets ‘c’, so take the diagonal 1 and add one: 2. A miss carries the best neighbour.
The corner reads 3: “ace”. One pass over the table, O(m·n) time. That’s 2-D DP.

name: Greedy
idea: Take the best move now. Never look back.
analogy: Cross a stream on stepping stones without ever planning the route. From each stone, only note the farthest stone you could land on. If the next stone sits past that mark, the crossing is impossible, and you knew without retracing a step.
whenToUse: A single choice now never needs revisiting
Only the best option so far matters
Brute force tries every combination

transcript.text: Five stones hold jumps of 2, 3, 1, 1 and 4. Can you reach the end? Trying every route from every stone blows up fast.
Forget the route. Track one number instead: the farthest stone you could reach so far.
Stone 1 jumps 3, landing on stone 4 and stretching the reach to 4. Every later stone sits inside it.
One scan, O(n) time: yes, you reach the end. That’s greedy: the best move now, never looking back.

name: Intervals
idea: Sort by start, then merge or split.
analogy: Lay every meeting of a shared day on one timeline in start order. Meetings that overlap or touch fuse into one busy block. What is left is the day’s true shape, with every gap visible.
whenToUse: Inputs are ranges with a start and end
Overlap or touching decides the answer
Order by start, then walk once

transcript.text: Four bookings cover 1–3, 2–6, 8–10 and 15–18. Which busy blocks do they really form? Comparing every pair is n² work.
Sort them by start instead. Once they line up, each booking only meets the block before it.
2–6 starts inside 1–3, so stretch the block to 1–6. 8–10 starts after 6, so it opens a new block.
One sort, one walk: O(n log n). Three blocks left: 1–6, 8–10 and 15–18. That’s intervals.
